idiom_name: impl Iterator (next() -> Option<Item>) + IntoIterator + lazy adaptor chains
implementation_notes: Rust makes the pattern a trait: a container implements IntoIterator and for loops desugar to into_iter()/next() until None, while the cursor is any type implementing Iterator with the single required method next() -> Option<Item>; the 70-odd provided methods (map/filter/take/zip/chain) return lazy wrapper adaptors, so a traversal is usually a chain of std adaptors and a hand-written cursor is just an impl Iterator for a struct holding the state. Because iterator state is owned and borrowed through the type system (for x in collection consumes it, .iter() borrows, .iter_mut() borrows mutably), the invalidation and aliasing bugs other languages catch at runtime are compile errors instead. The price is that adaptor chains are lazy (nothing runs without a consumer), the concrete adaptor type is unnameable (APIs return impl Iterator or Box<dyn Iterator>), and a chain over a &mut borrow pins that borrow for the loop.
pitfalls: Adaptors are lazy and #[must_use]: a chain built only for side effects (map with a print) does nothing until consumed, and dropping the result silently skips the work.

for x in collection moves the collection while for x in &collection borrows it; .iter()/.iter_mut()/into_iter() produce &T/&mut T/T respectively, and mixing them changes element types and ownership in ways the compiler reports far from the loop.

Returning iterators means naming an unnameable type: impl Iterator is static and allocation-free but must be a single concrete type with the right lifetime, while Box<dyn Iterator> erases the type at the cost of an allocation plus a lifetime bound.
Iterator::size_hint is a hint, not a contract: collect()/Vec::with_capacity trust it, and a miscomputed hint wastes memory or truncates a badly-behaved external iterator.
